articles.title: Italy fines Meta €805m over accessing users' photos
articles.summary: The social media giant is accused of not informing 20 million users it had access to their photos.
articles.body:
Italian regulators have fined social media giant Meta €805m (£670m; $887m) for accessing Android users' photos without their specific consent.

Italy's Data Protection Authority said Meta did not properly inform about 20 million smartphone users that it had access to their photos and videos via a feature of the Facebook app.

It has given Meta 60 days to disable the feature by default and seek users' consent separately.

The fine is among the largest an Italian authority has ever imposed on a tech giant.

A Meta spokesperson told the BBC that it planned to appeal.

The charge is related to a feature which suggests photos and videos from a user's phone gallery as ideas for posts.

Facebook requested access to users' photo galleries through a single app-wide authorisation. According to the Italian regulator, a preceding notice did not make clear that this would also allow Facebook to generate suggestions based on photos in their gallery.

The regulator said it took into account "the high number of people affected" and the fact it is "still ongoing for those who have not updated the app and for those who have already given their consent to the system".

It also cited "Meta's lack of co-operation".

Meta told the BBC: "We strongly disagree with the [regulator's] assessment of the facts, its application of the law, and the disproportionate level of the fine.

"This is a straightforward feature which helps people post photos and videos to Facebook. People must give permission on their device before it can operate, and they can change this permission at any time via their settings."

Last month, Meta, which is also behind Instagram and WhatsApp, was hit with its largest fine ever for its business practices.

A US judge in New Mexico ordered the company to pay $25bn (£18.6bn) after it found that found it had spent years lying to the public about how it handled Facebook user data.

articles.title: UK weather: Brief mild spell before more cold health alerts take effect
articles.summary: A short-lived milder spell is on the way for Sunday before more cold health alerts come into force.
articles.body:
Another round of cold health alerts is set to come into force on Sunday following a brief break from the weekend's subzero temperatures.

After readings dipped as low as minus 7C early on Saturday, most places on Sunday morning will be milder and free of frost.

Widespread rainfall is likely with hail and thunderstorms possible for parts of Wales and southern England.

Into the new week, the wintry chill is set to return with UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) cold-health alerts beginning for the north-east and north-west of England and Yorkshire and the Humber from 21:00 GMT on Sunday.

Milder air will arrive on Sunday morning, with temperatures sitting around 2 to 6C for most places, although the coldest spots in central and eastern England may still drop close to freezing.

It follows a bitter morning on Saturday with minus 7.2C recorded at South Newington in Oxfordshire - the lowest temperature of the autumn so far.

As weather fronts move in from the west, areas of showery rain will drift eastwards across much of the UK through the day.

The heaviest of the rain first thing is likely to be in Scotland and Northern Ireland as well as south-western parts of England and Wales.

Outbreaks of rain will then become widespread by the middle of the day, with a chance of thundery downpours in the south.

Some disruption is possible due to bursts of heavy rain. Trees will be shedding leaves readily due to the rain and the brisk winds, and these could block drains - leading to localised flooding.

Return of Arctic chill brings more cold health alerts

The slightly milder weather will not stick around long.

Beginning at 21:00 GMT on Sunday, UKHSA cold health alerts will come into effect for the north-east and north-west of England and Yorkshire and the Humber lasting until 09:00 GMT on Thursday.

As low pressure clears eastwards on Monday, rain and wind will ease, but colder air will again move in from the north bringing a return to frost and fog.

Temperatures on Monday afternoon will be around 5 to 8C across most of the UK with a noticeable wind chill near eastern coasts.

The exception will be the far southwest of England where highs may reach 12C ahead of the next Atlantic weather front bringing rain and wind.

Monday night's wet and windy weather will sweep across many parts of the country with gales likely around western coasts.

The rain may be preceded by a spell of sleet and snow across the high ground including Snowdonia, parts of the Pennines and in the Highlands. Elsewhere, it will be too mild for any wintry weather.

The remainder of the week will be a temperature rollercoaster with alternating spells of mild and cold weather. You can keep up to date with your local forecast by checking BBC Weather online and on the app .

articles.title: A Minnesota man reported chest pain during an in-person consultation and a virtual appointment three months later before dying from heart attack complications while exercising at home; his family wins an $84 million malpractice verdict against Fairview
articles.summary: A Hennepin County jury issued an $84 million malpractice verdict against Fairview Health Services on 29 September for the family of a 53-year-old man who
articles.body: A Hennepin County jury issued an $84 million malpractice verdict against Fairview Health Services on 29 September for the family of a 53-year-old man who died from heart attack complications after allegedly receiving an inadequate medical evaluation from a clinician at the hospital. It is one of the largest malpractice awards in the state’s history. Part of the award reflects what the man would have earned in the years ahead.Two consultations that failed to adequately address his chest painReece Devlin, 53, moved to Minneapolis from Australia and spent years as a partner at Ernst & Young. In October 2022, he went to an M Health Fairview Uptown clinic with chest pain, according to court records. A Fairview clinician ordered an electrocardiogram to check the electrical activity of Devlin’s heart. The practitioner stated that Devlin’s Mayo Clinic executive physical records had also been reviewed at the time. Brandon Thompson, the attorney who represented Reece Devlin’s wife and two children in the medical malpractice lawsuit against Fairview Health Services, argued that computer records contradicted this claim. The records reportedly showed that the practitioner had visited another patient and reviewed the records of 11 others instead. The attorney also argued that computer records contradicted the clinician’s claim that he had asked Devlin about his chest pain during a January 2023 virtual follow-up appointment, which had been scheduled to review his medication. He further said the evidence made jurors question whether Fairview had provided the required standard of medical care. The jury agreed. Without these medical records, the practitioner could not provide adequate medical care.Devlin died on 29 January 2023 while working out in his basement. This was less than a week after the virtual consultation.Medical malpractice cases often turn on what a clinician should have done. This one didn’t. The parties largely agreed on the standard of care for a patient with possibly serious chest pain. The dispute was over whether the evaluation met that standard.The family alleged that the physician assistant did not sufficiently investigate the complaint or review relevant prior records. They also said he did not tell Devlin that his chest pain could signal a serious heart problem. The family argued that the cardiac evaluation fell short of what his symptoms required.His widow and two children sued. The week-long trial ended with a Hennepin County jury awarding them $84 million against Fairview Health Services this autumn. “This is a stark reminder of the importance of being thorough, even when you’re busy, even when it’s a virtual visit,” Brandon Thompson told The Minnesota Star Tribune.In a written statement, Devlin’s wife said: “While nothing will ever undo the loss our family has suffered, we take comfort in the fact that we were able to tell our story, and the jury heard it loud and clear.”Fairview argued that it had conducted a thorough examination as required. During the trial, it did not comment on the verdict but expressed sympathy for the family. It said it could not comment further other than “to extend our deepest sympathies to Mr Devlin’s family for their loss. We respectfully disagree with the jury’s verdict and continue to believe the care provided was evidence-based.”Meanwhile, the verdict is not final. A judge can order a remittitur, which reduces an award the judge considers unsupported by the evidence, but the plaintiff must agree to it. Fairview can also appeal. A similar process cut a $110 million verdict against St Cloud Orthopedic Associates after a college student’s knee injury was allegedly mishandled. articles.title: Syria rolls back new entry restrictions on US, British citizens after Americans report being turned away
articles.summary: Syria has reversed a temporary requirement for American and British citizens to obtain prior approval before entering the country, restoring the earlier
articles.body: Syria has reversed a temporary requirement for American and British citizens to obtain prior approval before entering the country, restoring the earlier entry procedures following controversy over reports that US travellers were being denied entry at border crossings. The Syrian Foreign Ministry announced the decision on Friday, November 13, saying that the requirement for advance clearance had been withdrawn and that entry procedures for citizens of the two countries had returned to their previous arrangements.Deputy Foreign Minister for Consular Affairs Mohammad Yaqoub al-Omar told the state-run Syrian Arab News Agency that the prior approval requirement had been introduced as a temporary measure. He did not explain why the restriction had been imposed or why it was withdrawn. Al-Omar added that entry procedures for citizens of other countries remained unchanged.The reversal came a day after videos circulated on social media showing American travellers claiming they had been refused entry into Syria. The reports raised questions about whether Damascus had introduced fresh restrictions on foreign visitors.On Thursday, Mazen Alloush, director of international relations and cooperation at Syria's General Authority for Ports and Customs, confirmed that US citizens had recently been added to a list of nationalities requiring advance approval from the Interior Ministry. Alloush said that while visas were issued at border crossings, citizens of certain countries were required to obtain clearance from the relevant authorities before travelling.He clarified that the General Authority for Ports and Customs was responsible for implementing Interior Ministry instructions and did not decide which nationalities were subject to the additional requirement.Syrian authorities did not disclose how long the restriction had remained in force or explain why British citizens were also included in the reversal.What were the entry rules for Americans?Before the temporary restriction, US citizens could obtain a visa on arrival at Damascus International Airport or at designated land border crossings. The new requirement for advance approval created uncertainty for American travellers, particularly those who had already planned trips to the country.The US State Department's travel information has said that American citizens can obtain a 30-day visa on arrival for approximately $200 at Damascus airport or land crossings with Jordan and Lebanon. articles.title: US suggested Ukraine cede parts of Donbas to Russia to become part of NATO
articles.summary: Zelenskyy rejected the possibility of Ukraine committing to neutrality and said he refused to cede territory to Russia.
articles.body:
US negotiators have floated the idea that Ukraine should cede parts of eastern Donbas in exchange for NATO membership, Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said, after the latest rounds ⁠of Russia-Ukraine peace talks in Abu Dhabi and Ireland.

This is the first time the question of linking NATO membership to territorial concessions has been raised, Zelenskyy told reporters in remarks released by his office on Saturday.

“The Americans raised a question: ‘What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine withdraw from ⁠Donbas?” he said. “That is why I believe NATO is back on the agenda.”

Zelenskyy said the parts of the Donbas region in eastern Ukraine the US asked about were areas Russia does not control. The Ukrainian president said he refused to cede territory.

“[Russian President Vladimir] Putin’s desire to change borders in Europe is a fact. I am sure this is part of his concept of revising security guarantees in Europe,” he said. “This is dangerous because, in my view, it is precisely things like this that lead to wars or escalations.”

Putin has long said that Ukrainian membership of NATO is a red line for Moscow, citing the issue as one reason for launching Russia’s full-blown invasion in 2022.

Zelenskyy did say that if Ukraine received a comprehensive package, including security guarantees, military and reconstruction funds, and a recovery plan from the US and other partners, he would put the question about ceding parts of Donbas to a national referendum.

“If the American side confirms precisely this to us, together with other NATO partners, then I will ask our Ukrainian society what it thinks: do we accept it or not?” Zelenskyy said.

He stressed that any arrangement would not involve recognising occupied territories as Russian. Zelenskyy also rejected the possibility of Ukraine committing to neutrality, saying that would require changing the country’s constitution.

“If Putin expects Ukraine’s neutrality to be enshrined, that’s not going to happen,” he said. “We’re not in NATO right now anyway.”

Despite the diplomatic push to end the conflict, Russia and Ukraine reported numerous overnight attacks . Russian officials reported on Friday that about 1,200 Ukrainian drones were fired at the country, with oil infrastructure among the targets, while Ukraine reported attacks on a hospital and the port of Odesa.

At the summit in Ireland over recent days, EU leaders agreed that Europe’s team for any Ukraine peace talks would comprise five major military powers – non-EU member Britain plus France, Germany, Italy and Poland – as well as EU officials. They would hold talks ‌with ‌US and Ukrainian officials, but not with Russia.

articles.title: Bill Maher warns Democrats not to 'go back to bad ideas' after sweeping midterm victories
articles.summary: Comedian Bill Maher warns Democrats not to revive "bad ideas" like defunding the police after sweeping midterm wins on "Real Time" Friday.
articles.body: Comedian Bill Maher issued a preemptive warning to Democrats following their sweeping midterm election wins, urging the party not to mistake its victories for a mandate to revive "bad ideas" that could drive voters back to the GOP. "Now that Democrats won the election, let’s not get high on our own supply like the last crowd did and interpret the W as a sign to go back to bad ideas," he said during Friday's episode of "Real Time." As examples, the liberal comedian pointed to "defund the police" and a refusal to enforce shoplifting laws, arguing that such approaches hurt the people progressives claim to help. BILL MAHER WARNS DEMOCRATS THAT SOME ON FAR LEFT WANT 'COMMUNISM' AFTER MIDTERM SWEEP Maher also mocked progressives he described as the "lawn sign people," accusing them of using yard signs touting equality, science and kindness to advertise their moral superiority. "It's all well and good to declare yourself the morally enlightened ones, but when your policy ideas are based on how good they make you feel and not on how much good they actually do, that's when people lurch to the other even worse extreme," he said. JAMES CARVILLE CAUTIONS DEMOCRATS TO STAY AWAY FROM DEI POLICIES AFTER MIDTERM VICTORIES Criticizing policies in Democratic-led cities, Maher asked: ""Who benefited when you didn't enforce the laws against shoplifting? Who benefits when you give a homeless schizophrenic clean needles instead of forcing him into treatment?" Maher also criticized what he characterized as White liberals' approach to racial issues, joking: "I talked to every Black person in America and it turns out they kind of don't give a s---. Yeah. Turns out they're not waking up every day saying, ‘What can I do today to make sure white people feel better about themselves?’" Tim Graham, the executive editor of the Media Research Center’s NewsBusters blog, told Fox News Digital, "None of the elitist media are anywhere near the kind of tough-love advice counselor for Democrats, and especially not in public. If they wanted to tell Democrats that their gooey intentions aren't equivalent to outcomes, they'd do it off the record." Christian Toto, the editor of Hollywood in Toto, told Fox News Digital, "Bill Maher is the most refreshing, unexpected pundit on late-night TV. He calls balls and strikes while simultaneously copping to his liberal bona fides." Toto added that Maher is "a pariah of sorts within his industry" and predicted that the "modern Left will happily ignore his wisdom, likely at their political peril." Jason Mudd, CEO of Axia Public Relations, told Fox News Digital, "If the Democratic Party were my client, I’d advise them to remember this win was more about Trump than about the party. He added, "They should lean moderate to win over more voters. I’d also have trusted advisors with an objective or contrarian view screen each message before it goes public." Maher also criticized conservatives, arguing that Democrats won across several states in the midterms because voters have a history of shifting from one political extreme to another. He first rejected what he characterized as Democratic moral superiority, then criticized what he described as Republicans' embrace of "cruelty." "Republicans lost this election because no one wanted the pendulum to swing all the way to full a--hole, to cruelty," he said. "Yes, liberal virtue signaling had become tiresome, but did we have to go to vice signaling?" he added. BLUE WAVE NEARLY SWALLOWED SOME OF AMERICA'S REDDEST STATES AS ELECTION DATA EXPOSES GOP'S CLOSE CALLS Maher pointed to fatal shootings during immigration enforcement, cuts to the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) and other incidents as examples of what he believed caused the political pendulum to swing back to the left. "This is how you lose even Texas," he insisted, referring to wins for Democrats James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa in the longtime red stronghold. "Everything is a reaction to what went before," he added later. Maher's comments come as Republicans review their midterm losses and reassess the party's strategy ahead of the 2028 elections. articles.body: NEW DELHI: The United States must respect India's right to defend itself and maintain a zero-tolerance policy towards terrorism, former US secretary of state Antony Blinken said on Saturday.Describing Washington's ties with India and Pakistan as "fundamentally different", he said the relationship with New Delhi was global in nature, while engagement with Islamabad was largely regional.Speaking at the Hindustan Times Leadership Summit 2026 in New Delhi, Blinken said India was a major global force and shared broad strategic interests with the US."India is a global force," he said, adding that the relationship and shared interests between Washington and New Delhi were "really global in nature".In contrast, he described the US relationship with Pakistan as "regional", while noting that cooperation with Islamabad remained important in certain areas, particularly counter-terrorism."The relations with Pakistan are regional, and there are still going to be important areas where we need to do things with them, particularly, for example, when it comes to counter-terrorism, but these are fundamentally different relationships," he said, PTI reported."We have to have a zero-tolerance policy for terrorism. And that means that we have to have respect for India's right to defend itself," he added.Blinken said Washington's approach should include support for India's efforts to respond to attacks, alongside diplomatic efforts to prevent tensions between New Delhi and Islamabad from escalating.He said preventing a wider confrontation was particularly important because both countries possess nuclear weapons, which could have devastating consequences if used.Reflecting on the US's past engagement with Pakistan, Blinken said Washington's strategic interests during the Cold War and the war in Afghanistan may have made successive administrations less critical of Pakistan's civil-military establishment."And there's certainly an opportunity for the United States to do more," he added.On India-US relations, Blinken described the transformation in ties over the past few decades as a shift from estrangement to a strategic partnership. He said the relationship was built on shared strategic interests and strong people-to-people connections."We moved from estrangement to a genuine and, in some ways, unique partnership, built on a convergence of strategic interests. Of course, it is also underpinned by the profound people-to-people connections between our societies," he said.He identified emerging technologies as a key area for future cooperation, pointing to opportunities in space, quantum technology and artificial intelligence."The next step is tech cooperation, our ability to work in space, tech, quantum, and artificial intelligence," he said.On India's relationship with Russia, Blinken acknowledged the deep historical links between the two countries and said Washington did not expect New Delhi to end that partnership."There will be places where we don't have the same perspectives. For Russia, we understand there is deep history between India and Russia. So, we don't want them to end it," he said.Blinken also spoke about the changing global order and its implications for the United States, including how domestic political developments and the midterm elections could shape Washington's international engagement.He discussed the Donald Trump administration's approach to global affairs and the wider impact of shifts in US politics on its relationships with allies and partners.The conversation also covered conflicts in West Asia, including the ongoing confrontation involving the US, Israel and Iran, and the risks it poses to regional stability and international security.Blinken discussed the strategic importance of the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global energy supplies, and the consequences of any disruption to shipping through the waterway. articles.title: Eurovision Asia: Philippines wins continent's first song contest
articles.summary: Front-runner Carmelle emerges victorious with her women's empowerment anthem Sobra-Sobra.
articles.body:
The Philippines have won the very first Eurovision Song Contest Asia, hosted in Bangkok and with 11 countries vying for the title.

Nineteen-year-old singer Carmelle was always a front runner with her women's empowerment anthem Sobra-Sobra, complete with its catchy rap section.

She earned 211 points in total - 93 from the jury and 118 from the public vote - ahead of Thailand's MANG x DAOU in second place with 170 points.

There was a joyous atmosphere at the One Bangkok Arena as the crowd cheered the contestants and celebrated the popular winner.

Carmelle, the youngest contestant in the competition, was an obvious favourite with the juries and the public despite strong showings from several nations.

Other notable acts included MANG x DAOU, whose emotive duet Aroma elicited huge cheers from the home crowd.

Bangladeshi beatboxers Beatmosphere eschewed the traditional backing track, instead using their voices to replicate the sounds of drums and basslines.

And Laos's Thinla performed her crowd-pleasing song Bae in a traditional Lao hilltribe outfit.

However, the Laotian song had a unintentional second outing after the music video was played over an apparent technical issue during the broadcast - meaning it was the last song the audience heard before the vote.

The voting system worked much the same as the European Eurovison, with the public vote accounting for 50% of the result and the other 50% coming from the 11 national juries - with additional points awarded from a rest of the world vote.

Also performing during the broadcast was 2026 Eurovision Song Contest winner Dara from Bulgaria, who performed her winning song Bangaranga and new song Bad Idea.

Thai superstar Jeff Satur also made an appearance, hitting the high notes in his performance of Black Tie.

Eurovision in Asia was an idea that has been talked about for decades, but one that never seemed to materialise - despite many false starts - until now.

There is a huge enthusiasm here for Eurovision Asia, but a large number of the audience were established fans of the original contest from other countries and regions of the world.

Speaking after the show, fan Zelie Pereira - who travelled from Scotland to Thailand to attend - said she was "very happy" with Carmelle's win.

Korea, Vietnam and Laos also received praise from Pereira and her friends Michael Peters and Scarlett Massie, both from England.

"It was amazing, a very high standard," said Massie.

"The dance was amazing. The sets were amazing. The costumes were amazing. The singing was amazing. Incredible", Peters added.

They confidently declared that "Asia Vision" should be the name for next year's show.

For some, it seems the excitement for another edition is already building.

However the crowd at the One Bangkok Arena thinned out not long after the Philippines singer Carmelle lifted the trophy.

The arena was crowded, but not full, and it's still not clear how much commitment there is among regional broadcasters to keep the contest going and expand it to more than 11 countries.

articles.title: Russia must be held accountable for its crimes
articles.summary: Investigations by the International Criminal Court, United Nations and independent human rights organizations have created substantial proof.
articles.body:
Numerous reports allege that Russia is committing war crimes on a scale comparable to World War II. They reveal that the Russian army routinely tortures and kills Ukrainians taken prisoner and purposely targets civilian infrastructure, including apartment buildings, shopping malls, schools and utilities.

In the latest particularly disgusting display, Russian army units are reportedly hunting civilians with drones for sport. The Ukrainians refer to this as a “ human safari .”

Since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, international organizations, journalists, human rights groups and Ukrainian investigators have documented evidence of unlawful killings, torture, sexual violence, forced deportations, deliberate attacks on civilian infrastructure and widespread violations of international humanitarian law.

Holding Russian leaders accountable is important to provide justice to victims, establish a historical record and reinforce the principle that violations of the laws of war and humanitarian law should not go unpunished.

Human Rights Watch reported in December 2025 that Russian authorities and military forces systematically tortured Ukrainian prisoners of war using physical and psychological abuse and holding detainees in inhumane conditions. The United Nations reported that evidence collected from hundreds of former prisoners indicated an extensive pattern of torture intended to break prisoners psychologically and physically. Such treatment violates Geneva Conventions protections for prisoners of war.

International humanitarian law prohibits sexual violence against civilians and detainees. The U.N. Human Rights Office has reported over 1,000 cases of rape and sexual violence in areas occupied by Russian forces. Human Rights Watch has documented evidence of sexual violence in several territories occupied by Russian forces.

But the most egregious crime is what Russia is doing with Ukrainian children. The forced transfer and deportation of Ukraine’s children is a major area of international concern and a crime under several international conventions .

The Institute for the Study of War has documented extensive efforts to Russify Ukrainian children, which seem to be part of Putin’s effort to address Russia’s drastic population decline . Taking children from their homes and attempting to change their cultural identity or nationality during an armed conflict defies international laws designed to protect cultural heritage.

In March 2023, the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Russian President Vladimir Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova, Russia’s commissioner for Children’s Rights, over alleged unlawful deportation and transfer of over 20,000 Ukrainian children to Russia. According to the court, there are reasonable grounds to believe the suspects bore criminal responsibility for these acts.

In addition to Putin, the International Criminal Court has issued arrest warrants for Russian Minister of Defense Sergei Shoigu and Chief of the General Staff Valery Gerasimov, based on alleged responsibility for attacks against civilian infrastructure.

The scale of civilian suffering is ongoing and growing. According to the United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine, at least 2,514 civilians were killed and 12,142 injured during 2025, and civilian casualty rates have remained high throughout 2026. Since the beginning of the war , over 12,000 Ukrainian civilians have been verified as killed and about 25,000 injured.

Accountability for war crimes presents significant challenges. International courts must collect reliable evidence, establish individual responsibility and distinguish between intentional crimes and casualties resulting from lawful military operations. Nevertheless, investigations by the International Criminal Court, United Nations and independent human rights organizations have created substantial proof.

Documented atrocities in Ukraine highlight the importance of international humanitarian law. War does not eliminate legal protections for civilians or prisoners, and military necessity does not excuse torture, intentional attacks on civilians, summary execution or unlawful deportation.

Welcoming Russia back into the community of nations when this war ends should not be considered until the military and civilian leaders guilty of war crimes have been held to account. And inviting Russian officials to events held in the United States, and especially to the White House, is frankly disgraceful.

John Fairlamb, Ph.D., is a retired Army colonel who served for 45 years as a commissioned officer and Department of the Army civilian in a variety of Joint Service positions formulating and implementing national security strategies and policies.

articles.title: Filipino singer Carmelle storms to victory in Eurovision Asia debut in Bangkok
articles.summary: Filipino singer Carmelle won the first Asian edition of the Eurovision Song Contest on Saturday with a fiery performance of her dance-pop song “Sobra-Sobra.”
articles.body: BANGKOK — Filipino singer Carmelle won the first Asian edition of the Eurovision Song Contest on Saturday with a fiery performance of her dance-pop song “Sobra-Sobra.” The 19-year-old beat 10 other acts in the grand final in Bangkok, with the winner chosen through votes from national juries in participating countries and viewers worldwide. After her victory, Carmelle said her song celebrated female empowerment and was intended as “a tribute to all Filipino women.” “I made history, since this was the first time,” she told The Associated Press. “It’s such a big responsibility for me, because this one is a global stage, so thank you everybody who voted for me.” Thai duo Mang x Daou finished second with an energetic performance of the romantic pop song “Aroma.” Vietnam’s Tóc Tiên placed third with a lively, stylish rendition of “Em Tiên.” Malaysia’s Aina Abdul took fourth with her powerful ballad “Bluest Sky.” Thinla of Laos finished fifth with “Bae,” a playful dance track that had the audience dancing whenever it was replayed during the show. Bhutan, South Korea, Mongolia, Nepal, Cambodia and Bangladesh also competed. Contestants made their entrances aboard tuk-tuks, the motorized three-wheeled vehicles common in Bangkok’s tourist districts. They waved national flags as thousands of fans cheered inside the city-center venue. Bulgarian singer Dara appeared as a special guest, performing “Bangaranga,” the song with which she won the 70th Eurovision Song Contest in Vienna earlier this year. The European contest seeks to put music before politics but has repeatedly been caught up in international conflicts. Russia was expelled in 2022 following its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The Israel-Hamas war in Gaza has also roiled the competition, prompting protests outside contest venues and leading organizers to restrict political flag-waving. Five longtime participants — Spain, the Netherlands, Ireland, Iceland and Slovenia — boycotted this year’s European competition over Israel’s participation.

articles.title: As a teenager, Dave Hunter rigged a homemade radar to find buried bulls on his grandfather’s farm; now he uses ground-penetrating radar to find lost graves, and has helped an outback council uncover more than 600
articles.summary: As a teenager, Dave Hunter built a rudimentary radar device to locate buried bulls on his grandfather’s farm.
articles.body: As a teenager, Dave Hunter built a rudimentary radar device to locate buried bulls on his grandfather’s farm. Decades later, that childhood experiment has evolved into a career helping communities find forgotten burial sites without disturbing the ground. His latest project has helped an outback council in Australia uncover 658 previously unmarked graves across two cemeteries in far-west New South Wales.Hunter, known as ‘Dave the Grave Hunter’, was contracted by the Central Darling Shire Council in July 2025 to investigate possible lost graves at the Menindee and White Cliffs cemeteries. Using specialist ground-penetrating radar equipment, his company, Hunter Geophysics, identified more than 300 burial sites at each location. A local report put the final tally at 338 graves at White Cliffs and 320 at Menindee. The project was completed in September 2026, according to the council.The discoveries were made without digging up the sites. Instead, Hunter pushed a machine resembling a lawn mower across the cemetery grounds, scanning the soil for signs of old burial pits. The findings have allowed the council to mark and protect places that had gradually disappeared from records or lost their visible markers.From buried bulls to forgotten gravesHunter’s interest in what lies beneath the ground began on his grandfather’s farm in Rushworth, northern Victoria. As a teenager, he was asked to locate bulls that had been buried on the property. With no sophisticated equipment at hand, he put together a basic device using a multimeter.That early experiment eventually grew into an interest in geophysics. Hunter later studied archaeology at La Trobe University and developed crude geophysical equipment to locate the remains of old buildings and gardens beneath a school in Melbourne. He went on to establish Hunter Geophysics in 2009, building a business around locating buried features and unmarked graves.He now completes around 10 to 15 cemetery projects a year, according to ABC News. His work involves using ground-penetrating radar (GPR), a technology that sends radar waves into the earth and records the signals reflected by changes in underground structures.However, the equipment does not actually detect human remains. Hunter told ABC News that it identifies the hole originally dug for a burial, rather than a body or skeletal remains. The disturbed soil left behind when a grave is filled can create a detectable contrast with the surrounding ground. In a cemetery, the dimensions and depth of such a disturbance can help him assess whether it is likely to be a grave. Hunter cautioned that the process is not an exact science and requires interpretation of the data.Giving forgotten graves their place againThe discoveries in Menindee and White Cliffs are now helping the council preserve the cemeteries and work towards identifying the people buried there. Council cemetery officer Tammie McMaster has been speaking to residents and examining old records and archives in the hope of attaching names to the graves.The council has also considered extending the project to other communities in the region, including Wilcannia and Tilpa. The work is important not only for planning future burials but also for ensuring that existing graves are not accidentally disturbed.At White Cliffs, a large rock has been placed in the cemetery to accommodate memorial plaques. The newly identified sites can also be marked and protected, helping preserve the history of the people buried there.The challenge is not unique to the outback. Across Australia, old cemetery records have been lost, wooden headstones have deteriorated and burial locations have faded from community memory. Research by archaeologists has highlighted how ground-penetrating radar can help locate such sites without invasive excavation and Hunter has been able to help with that.You use AI every day. articles.title: Protest held over plan for Keswick data centre near nature site
articles.summary: The proposed Apex data centre at Keswick, near Norwich, would be powered by offshore wind.
articles.body:
Hundreds of people have taken part in a city centre protest against a proposed large data centre near a nature reserve.

Plans have been submitted for the Norwich Apex facility, whose 150MW energy needs would be powered by offshore wind .

One protester calling himself "Shivering Beetle" said: "I genuinely do not believe that this can have a positive impact on the environment."

Matt Bartram, chief executive of Norwich Apex, said: "We understand how important Norfolk's natural environment is to local people, and we take concerns about wildlife, trees and noise seriously."

He added: "Protecting the surrounding environment has been central to the design of our proposals from the outset."

The demonstration in Norwich took place as thousands of people held a protest in Edinburgh against the building of large-scale AI data centres.

The Norwich protesters expressed fears that the project in Keswick, just outside the city, could damage Marston Marshes and other wildlife areas.

Bartram told the BBC the plans included planting more than 15,000 new trees and creating about a mile of hedgerow.

"Existing trees, woodland and hedgerows will be retained and protected, with new habitats designed to support local wildlife, including bees and other pollinators," he said.

However, Shivering Beetle said new saplings were not equivalent to mature trees.

"Trees are going to take a long time to grow. After five years they don't have to keep them – they could just tear them up if it's too much ground-keeping."

Planning documents show the building off the A140 Ipswich Road would be about 20m high and would require 72 chiller units on its roof.

Shivering Beetle said: "With things like low-frequency humming that is emitted from data centres, the chances are that it's going to drive off a lot of species of different insects and animals."

He believes the scheme could "kill thousands of bees".

But Bartram said: "Independent ecological and acoustic assessments have informed the proposals, including measures to protect nearby nature reserves and minimise noise."

He said the design included "substantial acoustic screening", with noise levels remaining "at existing background levels at nearby sensitive locations".

Bartram believes the scheme is "a major opportunity for Norfolk", creating up to 150 permanent jobs as well as "essential digital infrastructure on which British businesses and public services increasingly depend".

"We believe economic progress and environmental responsibility can go hand in hand," he said.

Shivering Beetle said many local people would continue to oppose the plans, which could see construction begin next year.

"If Norwich Apex plan to push this through, [today's protest] means we've got enough people behind us to do a sit-in, to camp there, to chain ourselves to the fences – whatever we need to do to stop this data centre being built," he said.

articles.title: Pope Leo urges end to violence in Peru during visit to remote Andes town
articles.summary: In Santa Cruz de Succhabamba, the pope told people not to respond to injustice with brutality.
articles.body:
Pope Leo XIV has called for an end to the violence gripping Peru, urging people not to respond to injustice with brutality, as he visited communities he once served as bishop.

“We feel threatened by the uncertainty of widespread violence and by the unspeakable suffering that continues to afflict so many of our brothers and sisters, he said, speaking at his former cathedral in Chiclayo.

Peru’s homicide rate has nearly doubled over the past five years, from 5.8 to 10.7 per 100,000 people. Reported extortion cases rose from 2,421 in 2019 to 26,734 in 2025, according to official figures cited by The Associated Press.

Security was a top concern for Peruvians in the last election. Conservative President Keiko Jujimori took office in July after promising to tackle crime. She has since declared states of emergency, including in Lima in August, then in September in prisons holding inmates linked to criminal organisations.

She has also pursued closer ties with Washington, bringing Peru into the ‘Shield of the Americas,’ a US-led regional coalition formed to carry out joint military operations against drug cartels.

Later on Saturday, in the Andean town of Santa Cruz de Succhabamba with a population of about 6,000, about 20,000 people came to an outdoor Mass, where Leo also addressed violence in society.

“Selfishness, injustice and evil are not overcome by brutality, but by prayer, patience and perseverance in denouncing what is wrong, by making our pleas with determination and working diligently to bring about the necessary changes,” said the leader of the Roman Catholic church.

He also drew attention to the suffering of rural communities he used to serve, where migration and declining birth rates are emptying villages.

“Let us think, for example, of the suffering of those who are forced to leave their homeland in search of a better future for themselves and their families in the great coastal cities,” he said.

Originally from Chicago in the United States and formerly known as Robert Francis Prevost, Leo arrived in Santa Cruz de Succhabamba by helicopter and was welcomed by a local band singing “Pope Leo, welcome home.”

He’d made the journey to the remote area many times before during his time as bishop of Chiclayo from 2015 to 2023, driving himself along winding mountain roads in a pick-up truck.

The pope, who holds both US and Peruvian citizenship, spent about two decades working in Peru as a missionary priest and bishop.

articles.title: Memorial opens honoring victims of the 2015 Charleston church massacre
articles.summary: It took Alana Grant years to find the strength to set foot in the basement of Mother Emanuel AME Church in Charleston, where her grandfather, the Rev.
articles.body: It took Alana Grant years to find the strength to set foot in the basement of Mother Emanuel AME Church in Charleston, where her grandfather, the Rev. Daniel Lee Simmons, attended his final Bible study. Her fears have been replaced by gratitude and hope now that there is a completed memorial in a courtyard by the front door for the “Emanuel Nine,” the Black churchgoers killed by an avowed white supremacist in 2015. The memorial provides a public space where “people can go and remember really what happened here,” Alana Grant said as she and her husband, state Rep. Hamilton Grant, got their first look. On Saturday, the long-planned memorial at the South’s oldest African Methodist Episcopal Church opens to the public. Emphasizing remembrance and reflection, the marble memorial is anchored by a Fountain of Grace, symbolizing God’s eternal love and mercy. Water flows from a shallow basin etched with the names of the six women and three men slain. Two Fellowship Benches with curved backs, sheltering anyone seated, flank the fountain. There is also a Cross of Hope, signifying redemption in the wake of suffering. A garden honoring the five survivors will come next. The Rev. Eric Manning, co-chair of the Mother Emanuel Memorial Foundation board, hopes it will mean something to everyone. “I was actually standing out there the other day,” said Manning, who took over after pastor and state Sen. Clementa Pinckney was among those killed. “Just for a moment, a peace came over me.” How the memorial is helping victims’ families Grant sees the memorial as a place to inspire conversations with her three small children about their great-grandfather. Because the facts of the shooting have been so public, she doesn’t want them to hear more from someone else. “I spent a lot of time thinking about it and praying about it,” she said. “I do want them to go so that they can kind of see what even brought me to South Carolina.” Former North Carolina state senator and Charlotte City Councilman Malcolm Graham, whose sister Cynthia Graham Hurd died huddled under a desk in the fellowship hall, attended the 2023 groundbreaking. He has anticipated visiting the memorial to reflect on “all the good times Cindy and I had as kids growing up, and being at the church and going to Sunday school.” A library, scholarship and other awards now carry the name of the accomplished librarian. Now she’ll live on in the memorial, too. “She said before she died that I was the most famous person in the family,” Graham said. “She is the most famous person in our family and I still look up to her.” As for the survivors to be honored with a garden, Grant says their living with memories of the shooting is “nothing short of heroism.” “There are not a lot of spaces where you get to see the survivors. We as Black people have survived so much,” Grant said. A church memorial that can be something for everyone When a committee sought an architect in 2017, they heard from designers all over the world, said John Darby, another memorial foundation co-chair who runs a Charleston real estate development firm. The final candidates were not asked to submit design proposals, but instead give written responses to deep questions on topics like forgiveness. That unconventional request was very prescient, said Michael Arad, an architect on the 9/11 Memorial whose design was ultimately chosen. He wrote about his admiration for the victims’ families who offered forgiveness to the shooter. A white, Jewish New Yorker who had never visited South Carolina, Arad did a deep-dive into the community for more than a year after he was selected. Having lengthy conversations with members of the congregation and researching the church’s 200-year history was essential, he said, and while the 9/11 memorial was a bigger endeavor, this design wasn’t any less complex. “My job as a designer was to allow people who visit the site to see and hear what was here all along,” he said. “We understand who we are as Americans through stories like this, through our response.” Arad said he embraces emotionally weighted projects as “a tremendous privilege” and he “could not imagine turning down a project like this.” The foundation has raised around $25 million over the last decade for the memorial, garden and other costs, much of it from foundations, endowments and corporations, Darby said. “It was one of those things that people wanted to be a part of,” Darby said. “We don’t want it to be an expense to the church.” Memorial stirs hope to learn from hate and tragedy Established in 1818, Mother Emanuel was built by free and enslaved people. In the 20th century, the church became a place of resistance where the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. and other civil rights figures spoke. The Emanuel Nine’s families applauded in 2015 when Gov. Nikki Haley removed the Confederate battle flag from state buildings. But with Republicans stirring an angry backlash against diversity and equity efforts, Graham said “racism, hatred and discrimination continue to be this country’s Achilles’ heel.” Alana Grant has tried over the years to gather support for a hate crimes statute, and her husband is among the lawmakers who pushed legislation named for Pinckney that would add enhanced penalties for hate crimes to South Carolina’s criminal code. It failed to pass, even though a senator was among the Emanuel Nine. She sees this memorial as an opportunity to raise “generational awareness” so younger people will campaign against hate. Tourists still come to the church daily out of curiosity or sympathy, and could leave the memorial feeling inspired. “We want more than your thoughts and prayers. We want your advocacy,” she said.

articles.body: An ICE officer has been accused of sexually assaulting a 21-year-old Lebanese woman at a Texas immigration detention facility after allegedly offering to help her obtain a Green Card in exchange for sex. According to a Newsweek report, the woman, identified as Rahaf Ali Almerhij, who also goes by Lucy Wise, alleged that ICE deportation officer Markell Wallace sexually assaulted her while she was detained at the El Valle Detention Facility in Raymondville, Texas. She has also accused him of threatening to have her husband arrested and deported if she refused his advances.The allegations were detailed in a sworn declaration submitted to the DHS Office of Inspector General.Almerhij said Wallace took her into an isolated room at the detention facility, where he allegedly touched her sexually without her consent. She claimed he offered to help her secure permanent legal status in the US in return for sexual favours and gave her his personal phone number."I did not consent to any of this; I refused and told him to stop," she said in her declaration.DHS has denied the allegations. A department spokesperson told Newsweek that the claims of misconduct at the facility were false, while adding that allegations of misconduct were treated seriously and investigated when substantiated.Woman says ICE officer threatened to deport her husbandAlmerhij alleged that Wallace also threatened to have her husband, Sam Wise, jailed and deported if she refused his advances. Wise is a US lawful permanent resident and lives in Texas. She said she did not disclose the alleged sexual assault while she was in detention because she feared retaliation. Her husband said he learnt about the alleged incident in late August.Almerhij and her husband had previously raised concerns about her treatment at the detention centre, including allegations involving inadequate eye care and privacy violations. One complaint claimed that male employees could see female detainees while they were naked.On October 9, Wise filed sexual misconduct complaints with four DHS and ICE oversight offices. Almerhij submitted a sworn declaration the following day. On October 23, she met investigators from the DHS Office of Inspector General at a border crossing in Mission, Texas, and handed over a 59-page handwritten diary that she had maintained during her detention.According to DHS, Border Patrol arrested Almerhij on February 19, 2026. The department said she had entered the United States illegally in August 2024. Her husband said she had been studying nursing at Texas A&M University before her detention. articles.title: 341 candidates shortlisted at Bahraich job fair; MLA distributes offer letters
articles.summary: 341 candidates shortlisted at Bahraich job fair under UP Mission Rozgar; 17 firms interviewed 602. MLA Anupama Jaiswal distributed offer letters, promoted Employment Sangam Portal.
articles.body: Bahraich: As many as 341 candidates were shortlisted for jobs at a district-level employment fair organised under the Uttar Pradesh govt’s Mission Rozgar campaign at Shanti Devi Subhash Chandra Sushant PG College in Chakujot, Bahraich. A total of 17 private companies interviewed 602 candidates, while city MLA Anupama Jaiswal distributed offer letters to selected candidates.The MLA urged young people to register on the Employment Sangam Portal, operated by the Department of Employment, to access job opportunities in India and abroad.Addressing the candidates, Jaiswal encouraged them to work with dedication and honesty, saying no work was big or small. She also urged them to overcome negative thinking and make the best use of available opportunities.She said the Centre and Uttar Pradesh govts were implementing various schemes to promote employment and self-employment, helping young people become self-reliant and create jobs for others.District employment officer Sanjay Kumar briefed candidates about employment opportunities and the Employment Sangam Portal. Departments including industry, khadi and village industries, lead bank and labour also set up stalls to provide information about govt schemes and employment initiatives.
